lead: This unit is about how IoT devices talk: the radio standards, network stacks and messaging protocols that carry sensor data. After it you can place any IoT protocol on a layered map, read its frame or message flow, and choose between short-range, long-range and industrial options for a given job.
about: Unit 3 covers the rules that let IoT devices exchange data. Chapter 3.1 explains protocol standardization and the layered model. Chapter 3.2 gives IEEE 802.15.4, the low-power radio under many IoT standards. Chapter 3.3 builds ZigBee and Z-Wave on top of it. Chapter 3.4 covers Bluetooth and Bluetooth Low Energy. Chapter 3.5 adds IPv6 with 6LoWPAN and RPL routing. Chapter 3.6 moves up to MQTT publish-subscribe messaging. Chapter 3.7 compares long-range LPWAN: LoRaWAN and NB-IoT. Chapter 3.8 looks at industrial protocols SCADA, BACnet and WirelessHART. Chapter 3.9 closes with local service discovery: mDNS, DNS-SD and UPnP. Each chapter names the layer, the frame or message flow, and one worked numerical example.

chapters.idea: A protocol is a set of message rules; standardization makes devices from different vendors interoperable.
chapters.depth: Cover why IoT needs standards, de jure vs de facto standards, and the layered model from application down to radio. Name the main bodies: IETF, IEEE, ITU-T, ISO, oneM2M, OMA SpecWorks, Connectivity Standards Alliance, LoRa Alliance, GSMA. Cover issues with IoT standardization: too many options, profiles, IPR, security, constrained devices, gateway translation. Some syllabi call this 'protocol standardization for IoT'. Mention M2M, WSN, SCADA and RFID protocols only as examples; their details come later. Keep Metcalfe's law to one line: network value grows with the square of users.

figure.aria: A five-layer IoT protocol stack from application down to PHY, with example protocols at each layer.

chapters.example: A 4-layer IoT protocol stack adds 2 bytes at layer 1, 4 bytes at layer 2, 8 bytes at layer 3 and 20 bytes at layer 4. The application payload is 100 bytes. What is the total header overhead in bytes and as a percentage of the final packet? Answer: 34 bytes of overhead; final packet 134 bytes; overhead is 34/134 = 25.4%.
chapters.trap: Do not treat a protocol and a standard as the same thing. A standard may define many optional features, and a de facto protocol may have no formal standard.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, logical design and communication models.
chapters.leave: Detailed frame formats and mechanisms to Chapters 3.2 to 3.9; IoT architecture to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: IEEE 802.15.4 is the low-rate, low-power PHY and MAC layer used by ZigBee, 6LoWPAN and WirelessHART.
chapters.depth: Cover PHY bands: 868 MHz, 915 MHz and 2.4 GHz; modulation and rates: 20, 40 and 250 kbps; 16 channels at 2.4 GHz. Cover MAC: CSMA/CA, beacon-enabled superframe, CAP and CFP, guaranteed time slots, non-beacon mode. Cover topologies: star, peer-to-peer, cluster tree. Cover 16-bit short and 64-bit extended addresses, and frame types: beacon, data, ACK, MAC command. One line: this chapter completes the subject as the shared radio layer under ZigBee and 6LoWPAN. Some syllabi call it LR-WPAN.

figure.title: IEEE 802.15.4 PHY frame
figure.aria: An 802.15.4 frame shown left to right: preamble, start-of-frame delimiter, length, MAC frame and frame check sequence.

chapters.example: An 802.15.4 data frame has a 127-byte PSDU. It is sent at 250 kbps. What is the total time on air including the 4-byte preamble, 1-byte SFD and 1-byte length? Ignore inter-frame spacing. Answer: total bytes = 127 + 6 = 133 B; time = 133 × 8 / 250000 = 4.256 ms.
chapters.trap: Do not confuse the 127-byte PSDU with the full over-the-air frame; PHY adds preamble, SFD and length. Beacon-enabled and non-beacon networks behave differently.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 wireless sensor networks; Chapter 3.1 layered model.

chapters.idea: ZigBee builds a low-power mesh on 802.15.4 for control applications; Z-Wave is a competing sub-GHz home-automation mesh.
chapters.depth: Cover ZigBee stack: PHY and MAC from 802.15.4, NWK with tree, mesh and AODV-like routing, APS with endpoints and clusters, ZDO, application profiles such as Home Automation, Smart Energy and Light Link. Cover device roles: coordinator, router, end device; security: network key, trust center, APS layer security. Cover Z-Wave: ITU-T G.9959, sub-GHz bands, mesh, controller and slave roles, data rates. Compare range, data rate, interference and ecosystem. Some syllabi call ZigBee's application layer 'ZigBee profiles'.

figure.aria: The ZigBee stack from application profiles down through APS, NWK, MAC and PHY, with 802.15.4 at the bottom.

chapters.example: A ZigBee network has 1 coordinator, 4 routers and 20 end devices. Each router can accept 6 children and the coordinator can accept 6. Can all 20 end devices join directly? If 2 routers fail, how many end devices lose their parent? Answer: 5 parent nodes × 6 children = 30 slots, so yes. After 2 routers fail, 3 parent nodes × 6 = 18 slots, so 2 end devices lose their parent.
chapters.trap: ZigBee is not IP-based in its classic form; ZigBee IP is a separate profile. Z-Wave does not use 802.15.4. APS security protects application frames, while network security protects hops.
chapters.leave: 6LoWPAN and RPL to 3.5; BLE to 3.4; service discovery to 3.9.

chapters.idea: Classic Bluetooth is a short-range cable replacement; Bluetooth Low Energy is a low-power protocol for small, periodic data.
chapters.depth: Cover classic Bluetooth: 2.4 GHz, 79 channels, 1 Mbps, piconet with one master and up to seven active slaves, scatternet, profiles. Cover BLE: 40 channels with 3 advertising channels, GAP roles (broadcaster, observer, peripheral, central), GATT services and characteristics, advertising packets, connection interval from 7.5 ms to 4 s, MTU, BLE 5 features: 2 Mbps PHY, coded PHY for long range, extended advertising. Compare power, latency and throughput. Some syllabi call BLE 'Bluetooth Smart'.

figure.aria: A BLE connection setup: peripheral advertises, central scans, peripheral responds, central connects, then data events follow.

chapters.example: A BLE connection interval is 50 ms. In each connection event the central and peripheral exchange 4 packets, each carrying 20 bytes of application data. What is the maximum application throughput in kbps? Answer: 4 × 20 × 8 / 0.050 = 12800 bps = 12.8 kbps.
chapters.trap: BLE is not classic Bluetooth with a lower duty cycle; it has a different link layer. A short connection interval lowers latency but raises power. Throughput must include protocol overhead in real systems.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 layered model; Chapter 3.2 low-power radio for contrast.
chapters.leave: ZigBee and Z-Wave to 3.3; LPWAN to 3.7; service discovery to 3.9.

chapters.idea: 6LoWPAN adapts IPv6 to small 802.15.4 frames; RPL routes IPv6 packets through low-power lossy networks.
chapters.depth: Cover 6LoWPAN: adaptation layer between IPv6 and 802.15.4, header compression (IPHC), fragmentation, mesh-under vs route-over, neighbor discovery. Cover RPL: DODAG, root, rank, objective function, trickle timer, upward and downward routes. Name LOADng and AODV as alternatives. Cover constrained networks: low power, lossy links, small MTU. Some syllabi call 6LoWPAN 'IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks'.

figure.aria: An RPL DODAG tree with a root, two rank-1 routers and three end devices at ranks 2 and 3.

chapters.example: A 1280-byte IPv6 packet is sent over 802.15.4 frames. Each frame has a 127-byte PHY payload and 25 bytes of 6LoWPAN and MAC overhead. How many fragments are needed? Answer: usable payload = 127 − 25 = 102 B per frame; 1280 / 102 = 12.55, so 13 fragments.
chapters.trap: 6LoWPAN is an adaptation layer, not a routing protocol. RPL is a routing protocol, not an adaptation layer. Fragmentation adds headers and increases loss probability.
chapters.leave: MQTT to 3.6; service discovery to 3.9; IPv6 details to a networking course.

chapters.idea: MQTT is a publish-subscribe protocol where a broker routes messages by topic, decoupling senders and receivers.
chapters.depth: Cover broker and clients, topics and wildcards + and #, QoS 0, 1 and 2, retained messages, last will, keepalive, clean session, ports 1883 and 8883, TLS. Cover MQTT-SN for UDP and constrained nodes. Cover message flow for each QoS. Some syllabi call MQTT 'Message Queuing Telemetry Transport'.

figure.aria: QoS 1 MQTT flow: publisher sends PUBLISH to broker, broker acknowledges, broker forwards to subscriber, subscriber acknowledges.

chapters.example: A sensor publishes a 20-byte payload to topic home/room1/temp every 10 s with QoS 1. The MQTT fixed header is 2 bytes. The broker forwards each message to 3 subscribers. How many bytes per hour does the broker send to all subscribers? Ignore acknowledgements. Answer: 22 B per subscriber per message; 3 × 22 = 66 B per message; 360 messages per hour; 360 × 66 = 23760 B = 23.76 kB per hour.
chapters.trap: QoS 2 is exactly once between one client and the broker, not necessarily end-to-end to every subscriber. A retained message is stored by the broker, not queued for every future client forever. Wildcards: + matches one level, # matches all remaining levels.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 application layer; Chapter 3.5 IPv6 and 6LoWPAN for constrained transport.
chapters.leave: CoAP, AMQP, DDS and OPC-UA are only named in 3.1; not taught here. Security to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: LPWAN trades data rate for long range and long battery life; LoRaWAN uses unlicensed chirp radio, NB-IoT uses licensed LTE.
chapters.depth: Cover LPWAN criteria: long range, low rate, low power, many devices. Cover LoRa: chirp spread spectrum, spreading factors SF7 to SF12, bandwidth 125, 250 or 500 kHz, time on air. Cover LoRaWAN: classes A, B and C, architecture with end device, gateway, network server and application server, ADR, duty cycle, OTAA and ABP join. Cover NB-IoT: 3GPP Release 13, 180 kHz bandwidth, 15 kHz subcarriers, modes standalone, guard-band and in-band, coverage enhancement, PSM and eDRX, protocol stack: PHY, MAC, RLC, PDCP, RRC, NAS. Some syllabi call NB-IoT 'LTE Cat NB1'.

figure.title: LoRaWAN architecture
figure.aria: LoRaWAN chain: end devices send radio packets to a gateway, which forwards them to a network server and then an application server.

chapters.example: A LoRaWAN node uses spreading factor SF9 and bandwidth 125 kHz. Symbol duration T_s = 2^SF / BW. A packet has 8 preamble symbols and 40 payload symbols. What is the time on air in ms, ignoring other overhead? Answer: T_s = 512 / 125000 = 4.096 ms; total symbols = 48; time = 48 × 4.096 = 196.6 ms.
chapters.trap: LoRa is the physical layer; LoRaWAN is the network protocol. NB-IoT is not a LoRa variant; it uses licensed LTE spectrum. Class A is the default and has the lowest power.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2 low-power radio; Chapter 3.4 BLE for short-range contrast.
chapters.leave: LTE history and 5G to a communications course; security to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Industrial IoT uses SCADA for supervision, BACnet for buildings and WirelessHART for reliable wireless field networks.
chapters.depth: Cover SCADA: components RTU, PLC, HMI, historian, MTU; data acquisition and control; Modbus as an example. Cover BACnet: building automation objects and services, BACnet/IP and MS/TP, change of value. Cover WirelessHART: IEC 62591, 802.15.4 PHY, TDMA, channel hopping, mesh, gateway, security, superframe. Compare determinism, range and legacy support. Some syllabi call WirelessHART 'IEC 62591'.

figure.aria: WirelessHART stack: application, network, TDMA data link with channel hopping, and 802.15.4 PHY.

chapters.example: WirelessHART uses a 10 ms timeslot. A superframe has 100 timeslots. A device gets 3 timeslots per superframe, and each timeslot carries 80 bytes. What is the superframe duration and the device's effective data rate? Answer: duration = 100 × 10 ms = 1 s; data = 3 × 80 = 240 B per superframe; rate = 240 × 8 / 1 = 1920 bps = 1.92 kbps.
chapters.trap: SCADA is a system architecture, not a single protocol. BACnet is for building automation, not general IoT. WirelessHART uses TDMA and channel hopping, not CSMA/CA.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.2, IEEE 802.15.4; Unit 6 industrial IoT for context.
chapters.leave: Modbus and OPC-UA details to other units; IoT security to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Service discovery lets a device find services and their addresses on a local network without a central directory.
chapters.depth: Cover mDNS: multicast DNS on 224.0.0.251 and ff02::fb, port 5353, .local domain, query and response, caching, conflict resolution. Cover DNS-SD: PTR, SRV and TXT records, service instance names, browsing. Cover UPnP: SSDP discovery on 239.255.255.250:1900, description XML, SOAP control, GENA eventing. Name common implementations such as Avahi and Bonjour as examples, not as endorsements. Some syllabi call DNS-SD 'Bonjour'.

figure.aria: mDNS query and response: client asks for IPP printers, printer returns PTR, SRV and TXT records.

chapters.example: A laptop sends an mDNS query for _ipp._tcp.local. A printer replies with a PTR record pointing to MyPrinter._ipp._tcp.local, an SRV record giving port 631 and target printer.local, and a TXT record with txtvers=1. What three records are returned and what does each give the client? Answer: PTR gives the service instance name; SRV gives the port and host target; TXT gives service metadata.
chapters.trap: mDNS is a transport for DNS messages; DNS-SD is a record naming convention. UPnP discovery uses SSDP, not mDNS. Multicast does not cross routers unless configured.
chapters.leave: DNS basics to a networking course; cloud service discovery to Unit 5.
